claim: Bacterial infection of Drosophila females reduces oviposition.
source: We demonstrate that bacterial infection of Drosophila females reduces oviposition and that peptidoglycan, the component that activates Drosophila antibacterial response, is also the elicitor of this behavioral change.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding, which is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Peptidoglycan is the elicitor of infection-induced oviposition reduction in Drosophila.
source: We demonstrate that bacterial infection of Drosophila females reduces oviposition and that peptidoglycan, the component that activates Drosophila antibacterial response, is also the elicitor of this behavioral change.
evidence: The abstract states this explicitly, and Figure 1D and E show that injection of purified PGN phenocopies bacterial infection effects.

claim: Peptidoglycan regulates egg-laying rate by activating NF-κB signaling pathway in octopaminergic neurons.
source: We show that peptidoglycan regulates egg-laying rate by activating NF-κB signaling pathway in octopaminergic neurons and that, a dedicated peptidoglycan degrading enzyme acts in these neurons to buffer this behavioral response.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this mechanism, supported by data in Figures 5 and 6 showing NF-κB pathway involvement in octopaminergic neurons.

claim: A dedicated peptidoglycan degrading enzyme acts in octopaminergic neurons to buffer the behavioral response to infection.
source: We show that peptidoglycan regulates egg-laying rate by activating NF-κB signaling pathway in octopaminergic neurons and that, a dedicated peptidoglycan degrading enzyme acts in these neurons to buffer this behavioral response.
evidence: The abstract states this explicitly, and Figure 2 shows that PGRP-LBPD isoform specifically modulates this response.

claim: Innate immunity serves as a first-line defense against microbes in all metazoans.
source: Innate immunity, which is common to all metazoans, serves as a first-line defense against microbes.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Two NF-κB-dependent pathways, IMD and Toll, are the main signaling cascades that control immune gene induction in Drosophila.
source: Genetic screens have identified two NF-κB-dependent pathways, IMD and Toll, as the main signaling cascades that control immune gene induction in Drosophila (Buchon et al., 2014; Lemaitre et al., 1995, 1996; Ferrandon et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Both IMD and Toll pathways are activated by bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan (PGN).
source: Both pathways are activated by a unique ligand, the bacterial cell wall peptidoglycan (PGN).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: PGN from Gram-negative bacteria and bacilli preferentially activates the IMD pathway via PGRP-LC and PGRP-LE.
source: PGN from Gram-negative bacteria and bacilli preferentially activates the IMD pathway via its detection by two members of the same PeptidoGlycan Recognition Protein (PGRP) family, PGRP-LC and PGRP-LE.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with supporting citations.

claim: PGRP-LC functions as the transmembrane signaling receptor upstream of the IMD pathway.
source: While PGRP-LC functions as the transmembrane signaling receptor upstream of the IMD pathway, PGRP-LE is detecting PGN intracellularly (Bosco-Drayon et al., 2012; Choe et al., 2005; Gottar et al., 2002; Rämet et al., 2002; Kaneko et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior work.

claim: PGRP-LE detects PGN intracellularly.
source: While PGRP-LC functions as the transmembrane signaling receptor upstream of the IMD pathway, PGRP-LE is detecting PGN intracellularly (Bosco-Drayon et al., 2012; Choe et al., 2005; Gottar et al., 2002; Rämet et al., 2002; Kaneko et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior work.

claim: PGN from Gram-positive bacteria engages a Toll-dependent response involving PGRP-SA.
source: PGN from Gram-positive bacteria rather engages a Toll-dependent response involving a circulating PGRP as sensor, PGRP-SA (Michel et al., 2001; Leulier et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with supporting citations to prior work.

claim: Drosophila Toll has no capacity to directly bind microbial motifs.
source: Indeed, in contrast to mammalian Toll-Like-Receptors, Drosophila Toll has no capacity to directly bind microbial motifs (Brough et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated with a supporting citation.

claim: Drosophila avoid food contaminated by pathogenic bacteria by using an olfactory pathway tuned to Geosmin.
source: Stensmyr et al. demonstrated that Drosophila avoid food contaminated by pathogenic bacteria by using an olfactory pathway exquisitely tuned to a single microbial odor, Geosmin (Stensmyr et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Geosmin is produced by harmful microorganisms.
source: Produced by harmful microorganisms, Geosmin is detected by specific Drosophila olfactory sensory neurons which then transfer the message to higher brain centers.
evidence: This is stated as part of the description of the Geosmin avoidance pathway.

claim: Activation of the Geosmin olfactory circuit induces avoidance response and suppresses egg-laying and feeding behaviors.
source: Activation of this olfactory circuit ultimately induces an avoidance response, and suppresses egg-laying and feeding behaviors, thereby reducing the infection risk of both the adult flies and their offspring.
evidence: This is stated as part of the description of the Geosmin avoidance pathway.

claim: Direct exposure to bacteria impacts sleep patterns and induces hygienic grooming in Drosophila.
source: For instance, direct exposure to bacteria impacts sleep patterns and induces hygienic grooming (Kuo et al., 2010; Yanagawa et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Drosophila plastically increases the production of recombinant offspring in response to parasite infection.
source: In addition, Drosophila plastically increases the production of recombinant offspring in response to parasite infection (Singh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Septic injury with E. coli induces a strong egg-laying drop within 6 hr following infection.
source: Septic injury with a needle contaminated with the innocuous Gram-negative bacteria E. coli, induced a strong egg-laying drop within 6 hr following infection (Figure 1B and C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data shown in Figure 1B, 1C, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The difference in the number of eggs laid by infected versus non-infected wild-type females was no longer seen after 24 hr.
source: The difference in the number of eggs laid by infected versus non-infected wild-type females was no longer seen after 24 hr demonstrating that the effects are transient and reversible (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Bacteria-induced egg-laying drop was stronger and lasted longer in PGRP-LB mutants than in wild-type flies.
source: As for the immune response, bacteria-induced egg-laying drop was stronger and lasted longer in PGRP-LB mutants than in wild-type flies while the amount of bacteria within the animals were equivalent (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplements 1B, 2A and B) (Zaidman-Rémy et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplements 1B, 2A and B.

claim: The egg-laying reduction effect was dose-dependent.
source: This effect was dose-dependent and not observed after sterile wound or when flies were injected with water (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The egg-laying reduction effect was not observed after sterile wound or when flies were injected with water.
source: This effect was dose-dependent and not observed after sterile wound or when flies were injected with water (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1D and E.

claim: The effects of bacterial infection on egg-laying were due to the presence of bacteria in the body cavity and not to cuticle wounding.
source: This demonstrates that the effects were due to the presence of the bacteria in the body cavity and not to cuticle wounding (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Egg-laying reduction was observed when flies were orally infected with bacteria.
source: Egg-laying reduction was also observed when flies were orally infected with bacteria and when flies mutant for another IMD pathway antagonist, Pirk, were infected (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Egg-laying reduction was observed when flies mutant for Pirk were infected.
source: Egg-laying reduction was also observed when flies were orally infected with bacteria and when flies mutant for another IMD pathway antagonist, Pirk, were infected (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: Injection of highly purified E. coli PGN in both wild type and PGRP-LB mutants fully phenocopied the effects seen with injection of bacteria.
source: Importantly, injection of highly purified E. coli PGN in both wild type and PGRP-LB mutants fully phenocopied the effects seen with injection of bacteria (Figure 1D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Mutants for Relish (RelE20) did not present egg-laying drop 6 hr post-infection.
source: Mutants for the transcription factor Relish (RelE20) and for the caspase Dredd (DreddD55) did not present egg-laying drop 6 hr post-infection (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1F.

claim: Mutants for Dredd (DreddD55) did not present egg-laying drop 6 hr post-infection.
source: Mutants for the transcription factor Relish (RelE20) and for the caspase Dredd (DreddD55) did not present egg-laying drop 6 hr post-infection (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1F.

claim: Inactivation of Relish, Dredd or PGRP-LE, but not PGRP-LC, completely suppressed the PGRP-LB-dependent egg-laying drop.
source: In addition, we performed epistasic analyses with PGRP-LB mutants and demonstrated that inactivation of, Relish, Dredd or the intracytoplasmic receptor PGRP-LE, but not the transmembrane protein PGRP-LC, completely suppressed the PGRP-LB-dependent egg-laying drop (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1G.

claim: PGRP-LE-dependent PGN detection induces a reduction of female oviposition by triggering NF-κB pathway activation.
source: Altogether these results demonstrate that PGRP-LE-dependent PGN detection by the fly induces a reduction of female oviposition by triggering NF-κB pathway activation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Six hours post-exposure to E. coli, ovaries from wild-type flies contained three-times more mature stage 14 oocytes than uninfected animals.
source: Six hours post-exposure to E. coli, ovaries from wild-type flies contained three-times more mature stage 14 oocytes than uninfected animals and less stage 10 immature oocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B and C.

claim: Six hours post-exposure to E. coli, ovaries from wild-type flies contained less stage 10 immature oocytes than uninfected animals.
source: Six hours post-exposure to E. coli, ovaries from wild-type flies contained three-times more mature stage 14 oocytes than uninfected animals and less stage 10 immature oocytes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A, B and C.

claim: Exposure to bacteria does not prevent oocyte maturation in the ovaries but rather blocks egg release into the oviducts.
source: Egg-laying drop was reversible by 24 hr suggesting that the exposure to bacteria does not prevent oocyte maturation in the ovaries but rather blocks egg release into the oviducts, leading to an accumulation of mature oocytes in ovaries of infected flies.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that egg-laying recovers by 24 hr and that mature oocytes accumulate.

claim: Antibody staining against activated-caspase (DCP1) did not reveal any sign of increased apoptosis in ovaries from infected females compared to controls.
source: Antibody staining against activated-caspase (DCP1) did not reveal any sign of increased apoptosis in ovaries from infected females compared to controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C and D.

claim: The presence of bacteria within the female body cavity induces a transient retention of mature oocytes within the ovaries leading to a drop of egg laying.
source: These results demonstrate that the presence of bacteria within the female body cavity induces a transient retention of mature oocytes within the ovaries leading to a drop of egg laying.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Bacterial infection did not impair adult feeding behavior in both wild-type and Relish mutants 6 hr after bacterial pricking.
source: As shown Figure 1—figure supplement 3E, bacterial infection did not impair adult feeding behavior in both wild-type and Relish mutants 6 hr after bacterial pricking.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claim: The PGRP-LB locus generates three protein isoforms (PGRP-LB PA, PC, PD) that all have in common the enzymatic amidase domain.
source: Interestingly, the PGRP-LB locus generates three protein isoforms (PGRP-LB PA, PC, PD) that all have in common the enzymatic amidase domain (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: The secreted PGRP-LBPC cleaves the PGN in the extracellular space.
source: While the secreted PGRP-LBPC cleaves the PGN in the extracellular space (Paredes et al., 2011; Zaidman-Rémy et al., 2006), the site and mode of action of the two other isoforms are unknown.
evidence: This is stated with citations to prior work.

claim: Neither PGRP-LBPA nor PGRP-LBPD possess a signal peptide, suggesting that they could act intracellularly.
source: In contrast to PGRP-LBPC, neither PGRP-LBPA nor PGRP-LBPD possess a signal peptide, suggesting that they could act intracellularly.
evidence: This is stated as an inference based on the absence of signal peptides.

claim: Only pLB1Gal4/UAS-PGRP-LBPD was able to fully rescue the egg-laying defect of PGRP-LB-infected females.
source: Surprisingly, out of the nine possible combinations, only pLB1Gal4/UAS-PGRP-LBPD was able to fully rescue the egg-laying defect of PGRP-LB-infected females (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2B.

claim: All three PGRP-LB isoforms retain the ability to cleave PGN.
source: In order to show that the three isoforms retain the ability to cleave PGN, we orally infected PGRP-LB mutants that ectopically expressed the different PGRP-LB isoforms in gut cells and monitored the expression of the IMD target gene Diptericin. The exacerbated Diptericin expression measured in PGRP-LB mutant was strongly reduced by expressing any of the three isoforms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) (Zaidman-Rémy et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: PGRP-LB isoforms are functionally equivalent in the regulation of gut immune response to bacteria.
source: These results suggest that although PGRP-LB isoforms are functionally equivalent in the regulation of gut immune response to bacteria, they have specific roles in regulating bacteria-induced egg-laying phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: PGRP-LB isoforms have specific roles in regulating bacteria-induced egg-laying phenotype.
source: These results suggest that although PGRP-LB isoforms are functionally equivalent in the regulation of gut immune response to bacteria, they have specific roles in regulating bacteria-induced egg-laying phenotype.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: PGRP-LBPD-specific mutants behave as wild-type flies as far as the immune response is concerned.
source: Although these mutants behave as wild-type flies as far as the immune response is concerned (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), their oviposition phenotype post-infection is identical to that of PGRP-LB null females (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PGRP-LBPD-specific mutants have an oviposition phenotype post-infection identical to that of PGRP-LB null females.
source: Although these mutants behave as wild-type flies as far as the immune response is concerned (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), their oviposition phenotype post-infection is identical to that of PGRP-LB null females (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 2C.

claim: Egg laying is controlled intracellularly in the pLB1-positive cells via the PGRP-LBPD isoform.
source: However, these two regulations are genetically distinct with egg laying probably controlled intracellularly in the pLB1-positive cells via the PGRP-LBPD isoform and immunity extracellularly by the PGRP-LBPC isoform.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Immunity is controlled extracellularly by the PGRP-LBPC isoform.
source: However, these two regulations are genetically distinct with egg laying probably controlled intracellularly in the pLB1-positive cells via the PGRP-LBPD isoform and immunity extracellularly by the PGRP-LBPC isoform.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data and prior knowledge.

claim: RNAi-mediated inactivation of either Relish or PGRP-LE in pLB1 cells was sufficient to block the effect of bacteria on female egg-laying behavior.
source: RNAi-mediated inactivation of either Relish or PGRP-LE in pLB1 cells was indeed sufficient to block the effect of bacteria on female egg-laying behavior (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3A.

claim: RNAi-mediated inactivation of Fadd in pLB1 cells blocked the effect of bacteria on egg-laying in the PGRP-LB mutant background.
source: Similar effects using RNAi-mediated inactivation of Fadd were observed in the PGRP-LB mutant background (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3B.

claim: IMD pathway activation via PGRP-LE in pLB1 cells is responsible for the oviposition decrease post-infection.
source: These results demonstrate that IMD pathway activation via PGRP-LE in pLB1 cells is responsible for the oviposition decrease post-infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: GFP staining from pLB1QF/QUAS-GFP reporter line was detected in neuronal-like fibers in the lateral and common oviducts.
source: GFP staining was detected in neuronal-like fibers in the lateral and common oviducts where it seems to connect the oviduct to the basal part of the ovaries (Figure 4A''').
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A'''.

claim: pLB1 projections were specifically detected in the posterior part of the ventral nerve cord, in the abdominal ganglion and in the subesophageal ganglion of the brain.
source: Projections were also specifically detected in the posterior part of the ventral nerve cord, in the abdominal ganglion and in the subesophageal ganglion of the brain (Figure 4A' and A'').
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A' and A''.

claim: PGRP-LB females in which the UAS-PGRP-LBPD construct was driven by the pan-neuronal Gal4 driver (elavGal4) no longer show a drop in egg-laying post-infection.
source: PGRP-LB females in which the UAS-PGRP-LBPD construct was driven by the pan-neuronal Gal4 driver (elavGal4) no longer show a drop in egg-laying post-infection (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5A.

claim: RNAi-mediated inactivation of IMD pathway component Relish or Fadd in neurons completely suppressed egg-laying drop post-infection.
source: In addition, RNAi-mediated inactivation of IMD pathway component Relish or Fadd completely suppressed egg-laying drop post-infection (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5B.

claim: Expression of Tetanous toxin (TTX) in pLB1 cells of mated uninfected females caused a strong defect in oviposition.
source: When TTX was expressed in pLB1 cells of mated uninfected females, a strong defect in oviposition was observed (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5C.

claim: Expression of TTX in pLB3-positive cells did not cause a defect in oviposition.
source: This was not the case when TTX was expressed in pLB3-positive cells.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be inferred from Figure 5C.

claim: Expressing the TRPA1 channel in pLB1 cells at permissive temperature (29°C) caused females to lay significantly more eggs than controls.
source: In contrast, pLB1Gal4/UAS-TRPA1 females raised at permissive temperature (29°C) laid significantly more eggs than controls (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5D.

claim: TRPA1 expression in pLB2 or pLB3 cells did not affect oviposition.
source: Such an effect of TRPA1 expression on oviposition was not observed when other pLBGal4 drivers were used (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5D.

claim: NF-κB pathway inactivation using entero-endocrine cell drivers (voila-Gal4 and prospero-Gal4) did not interfere with egg-laying behavior.
source: NF-κB pathway inactivation using two entero-endocrine cells drivers, voila-Gal4 and prospero-Gal4, did not interfere with egg-laying behavior (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: In neurons, the IMD pathway is modulated by the PGRP-LBPD isoform to fine tune the oviposition drop following exposure to bacteria.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that pLB1 cells activity impacts oviposition and that in neurons, the IMD pathway is modulated by the PGRP-LBPD isoform to fine tune the oviposition drop following exposure to bacteria.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Fadd RNAi overexpression in ILP7 and ppk-positive neurons did not prevent egg-laying drop post-infection.
source: However, as shown Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, Fadd RNAi overexpression in these neurons did not prevent egg-laying drop post-infection.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Overexpression of the SPR cDNA under the pLB1Gal4 driver was not sufficient to rescue egg-laying behavior of SPR null mutants.
source: In addition, overexpression of the SPR cDNA under the pLB1Gal4 driver was not sufficient to rescue egg-laying behavior of SPR null mutants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Bacterial infection affects egg-laying behavior of virgin females.
source: However, virgin females also produce unfertilized mature oocytes that they released regularly. Importantly, using PGRP-LB mutants, we noticed that bacterial infection was also affecting egg-laying behavior of virgin females (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6A.

claim: Inactivation of pLB1 cells via TTX overexpression impacted wild-type virgin females oviposition rate.
source: Moreover, we could show that inactivation of pLB1, but not of pLB3 cells via TTX overexpression impacted wild-type virgin females oviposition rate (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6B.

claim: pLB1Gal4/UAS-TTX virgin females presented ovaries packed with stalled mature oocytes.
source: pLB1Gal4/UAS-TTX virgin females presented ovaries packed with stalled mature oocytes which led to an important increase of ovaries size and, in turn, of female abdomen (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B and C.

claim: The phenotypes of pLB1Gal4/UAS-TTX virgin females are reminiscent of those seen in mutants for the octopamine pathway (TβHnM18).
source: Both phenotypes are reminiscent of those seen in mutants for the octopamine pathway (TβHnM18, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C) or in flies in which octopaminergic neurons are functionally inactivated (Monastirioti et al., 1995).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: RNAi-mediated NF-κB pathway inactivation in TβH-positive cells only was sufficient to prevent the bacterially induced egg-laying drop in wild-type and PGRP-LB mutant background.
source: As shown in Figure 6C and D, RNAi-mediated NF-κB pathway inactivation in TβH-positive cells only, was sufficient to prevent the bacterially induced egg-laying drop in wild-type and PGRP-LB mutant background.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6C and D.

claim: PGRP-LBPD ectopic expression under the Tdc and the TβH Gal4 drivers was sufficient to rescue PGRP-LB mutant egg-laying phenotype.
source: As shown Figure 6E, PGRP-LBPD ectopic expression under the Tdc and the TβH Gal4 drivers, was sufficient to rescue PGRP-LB mutant egg-laying phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6E.

claim: Providing an excess of TβH in pLB1 cells was sufficient to fully rescue PGRP-LB oviposition drop following infection.
source: Providing an excess of TβH in pLB1, but neither in pLB2 nor in pLB3 cells, was sufficient to fully rescue PGRP-LB oviposition drop following infection (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 6F.

claim: Bacterial infection induces in neurons a NF-κB-pathway-dependent regulation of octopaminergic signal which in turns modulates ovulation and triggers a reduction of female oviposition.
source: Altogether these results indicate that bacterial infection induces in neurons a NF-κB-pathway-dependent regulation of octopaminergic signal which in turns modulates ovulation and triggers a reduction of female oviposition.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Bacteria derived PGN entry into the fly body cavity activates innate immune response in fat body cells.
source: Our present data demonstrate that bacteria derived PGN entry into the fly body cavity has, at least, two physiological consequences (Figure 7). In addition to activate innate immune response in fat body cells, it also blocks mature egg delivery in oviduct and hence reduces egg laying of infected females.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: Bacteria derived PGN entry into the fly body cavity blocks mature egg delivery in oviduct and reduces egg laying of infected females.
source: Our present data demonstrate that bacteria derived PGN entry into the fly body cavity has, at least, two physiological consequences (Figure 7). In addition to activate innate immune response in fat body cells, it also blocks mature egg delivery in oviduct and hence reduces egg laying of infected females.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and illustrated in Figure 7.

claim: This bacterially induced behavioral change is due to an NF-κB pathway-dependent modulation in octopaminergic neurons.
source: We further demonstrate that this bacterially induced behavioral change is due to an NF-κB pathway-dependent modulation in octopaminergic neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: Both immune and behavioral responses are fine-tuned by distinct and specific PGN degrading enzymes.
source: We finally present evidence that both responses, that are potentially detrimental if not down-regulated, are fine-tuned by distinct and specific PGN degrading enzymes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: By regulating the level of internal PGN, flies adapt their egg-laying behavior to environmental conditions.
source: We propose that by regulating the level of internal PGN, flies adapt their egg-laying behavior to environmental conditions.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental findings.

claim: PGRP-LB ensures that low level of PGN does not affect egg laying in standard environmental conditions.
source: In standard environmental conditions, PGRP-LB ensures that low level of PGN does not affect egg laying.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claim: When PGN concentration reaches a certain threshold, NF-κB pathway activation in neurons blocks egg release.
source: However, whenever PGN concentration reaches a certain threshold, which either reflects an infection status or the presence of a highly contaminated food supply, NF-κB pathway activation in neurons is blocking egg release.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model.

claim: PGN of ingested bacteria is capable of reaching the internal fluid and triggering dedicated signaling cascades.
source: As PGN of ingested bacteria is capable of reaching the internal fluid and triggering dedicated signaling cascades (Basset et al., 2000), one could imagine that such a mechanism prevents flies to lay their eggs in highly contaminated food in which their development and that of the hatching larvae could be impaired by microbes.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: PGRP-LB mediated PGN scavenging is crucial since a non-regulated behavioral immune response would lead to a severe drop in the amount of progeny.
source: In this context, PGRP-LB mediated PGN scavenging is crucial since a non-regulated behavioral immune response would lead to a severe drop in the amount of progeny which may not be in keeping with the real threat.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: Blocking the energy-consuming egg production in infected flies could be a way for them to mobilize resources required for full activation of innate immune defences.
source: Blocking the energy-consuming egg production in infected flies could be a way for them to mobilize resources required for full activation of innate immune defences.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the findings.

claim: A similar depression of oviposition has been documented in female flies exposed to parasitoid wasps.
source: A similar depression of oviposition has recently been documented in females flies exposed to parasitoid wasps who lay their eggs in Drosophila larvae (Kacsoh et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated with a citation to prior work.

claim: Visual perception of wasps by female flies induces a long-term decline in oviposition associated with an early stage-specific oocyte apoptosis.
source: However, while visual perception of wasps by female flies induces a long-term decline in oviposition associated with an early stage-specific oocyte apoptosis, PGN effects are transient and rather lead to a late stage oocyte accumulation suggesting that although the final outcome is the same, the mechanisms differ.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to prior work.

claim: PGN effects on oviposition are transient and lead to a late stage oocyte accumulation.
source: However, while visual perception of wasps by female flies induces a long-term decline in oviposition associated with an early stage-specific oocyte apoptosis, PGN effects are transient and rather lead to a late stage oocyte accumulation suggesting that although the final outcome is the same, the mechanisms differ.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to prior work and supported by experimental data.

claim: PGN sensing acts on egg-laying behavior via neuronal modulation.
source: The present data indicate that PGN sensing acts on egg-laying behavior via neuronal modulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: NF-κB pathway signaling in octopaminergic neurons is the actor of PGN-dependent oviposition reduction.
source: We identified NF-κB pathway signaling in octopaminergic neurons as the actor of this PGN-dependent oviposition reduction.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Octopaminergic neurons innervate numerous areas in the brain and in the thoraco-abdominal ganglion and project to various reproductive structures.
source: Likewise, octopaminergic neurons have been shown to innervate numerous areas in the brain and in the thoraco-abdominal ganglion and to project to various reproductive structures such as ovaries, oviducts and uterus, further work will be needed to exactly pinpoint the identity of the affected octopaminergic neurons, their targets and their effect on fly behavior.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge.

claim: The NF-κB protein itself is required for the behavioral response to infection.
source: Knowing the NF-κB protein itself is required for this behavioral response and that increasing the amount of available octopamine via overexpression of the TβH enzyme rescues the oviposition drop, it is expected that IMD pathway activation in neurons will have transcriptional consequences.
evidence: This is stated based on the experimental findings.

claim: Increasing the amount of available octopamine via overexpression of the TβH enzyme rescues the oviposition drop.
source: Knowing the NF-κB protein itself is required for this behavioral response and that increasing the amount of available octopamine via overexpression of the TβH enzyme rescues the oviposition drop, it is expected that IMD pathway activation in neurons will have transcriptional consequences.
evidence: This is stated based on the experimental findings shown in Figure 6F.

claim: Dorsal, a member of the Toll NF-κB signaling cascade, has been shown to function post-transcriptionally together with IκB and IRAK at the post-synaptic membrane to specify glutamate receptor density.

claim: Drosophila uses a unique bacteria associated molecular pattern to activate different processes related to host defence.
source: We show here that Drosophila uses an unique bacteria associated molecular pattern to activate different processes related to host defence, namely the production of antimicrobial peptides and the modulation of oviposition behavior.

claim: Different isoforms of the same PGN scavenging enzyme, PGRP-LB, are required to fine-tune immune and behavioral responses.

claim: The secreted PGRP-LBPC isoform acts non cell-autonomously to dampen immune activation by circulating PGN.

claim: The behavioral response to infection is not transmitted via PGRP-LC but rather by the intracytoplasmic PGRP-LE receptor.
source: Even more remarkable, this response is not transmitted via PGRP-LC but rather by the intracytoplasmic PGRP-LE receptor.

claim: PGRP-LE is regulating response to bacteria in some part of the gut.

claim: PGN, when ingested or introduced into the body cavity, not only activates antibacterial immune response but also influences neuronally controlled behaviors in flies.
source: In essence, our results demonstrate that PGN, when ingested or introduced into the body cavity, not only activates antibacterial immune response but also influences neuronally controlled behaviors in flies.

claim: The sickness behavior deciphered does not appear to be a side effect of an energetically expensive immune response, but rather the result of a specific regulation.
